chunk_findings.detail:
`ItemEdit.queue` is only forwarded on the non-worktree path:

```python
    if edit.worktree is not None:
        return _update_and_rebind(repo, log, cfg, item, fields, edit.worktree)   # no queue
    return _record_update(log, cfg, it, fields, queue=edit.queue)
```

`_update_and_rebind` receives only `fields` (and the worktree path), never `edit.queue`, and it is the only other place a glob/resource re-target happens. So given the input `ddflow update --item X --globs help.py --queue --worktree WT`, the code takes the early return at line 84, `_waiting(...)` (the sole caller of `WG.register`/`WG.release_advice`) is never reached, no `waiting_on` record is registered for the requested glob, and the cycle/release advice machinery never fires for this update. Two agents each widening onto a glob the other holds will therefore both keep their old leases and poll forever — the exact hold-and-wait deadlock this change exists to remove — silently, because `--queue` is accepted by the model but has no effect on this path. Same for `claim` if it routes through this entry point.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items.py:84 (update / _update_and_rebind)

chunk_findings.detail: A claim refused because a queued waiter is ahead (`_refuse_if_queued` returning `O.refused(..., queued_behind=...)`) never calls `_record_waiting`; the only registration site is the `except` branch in `_acquire` around the `L.acquire` live-holder refusal. So waiters that are merely *behind the queue* get no `waiting_on` record: no `since`, no participation in `WG`'s cycle detection, and no `[lease].wait_max_s` release. Concrete failure: C claims `h.py` (held by A) and is recorded waiting for it. B then claims `h.py` with `--queue`; it is refused "queued behind C" and is *not* recorded. Meanwhile A claims `g1` (held by B), is refused by `L.acquire`, and is recorded waiting for B. The cycle A→B→A now exists, but on A's registration the second refusal cannot see B because B has no record, so `DX-lease-wait-cycle` detection never fires and the pair sits in hold-and-wait. The regression test ("two items that each want a glob the other holds are detected on the second refusal") only passes as long as neither party was ever told it was queued behind a third party; add a third waiter and detection silently stops working.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim.py:_refuse_if_queued

chunk_findings.detail: The queue-ahead check is skipped whenever the item already held a lease (`held_before`) or `force` is set — i.e. exactly the widening case the change is about. A widening claim therefore bypasses FIFO and can take a glob a waiter queued for. Concrete failure: agent W queues for `g.py`, which item Z holds, so W is recorded waiting for `g.py` (since t0). When Z releases `g.py`, item X — which already holds its own lease `h.py` and is now widening to `g.py` — calls claim with `want=[g.py]`; `held_before` is true, so `_refuse_if_queued` returns `None`, `L.acquire` finds no live holder and succeeds, and X takes `g.py` even though W is ahead in the queue. W's next attempt is refused again, so the waiter is starved and the hold-and-wait the change aims to break is re-introduced for holders. (The same `skip` makes `force`/update widening bypass the queue entirely.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/claim.py:_refuse_if_queued call site (`skip=force or held_before`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The change binds `waits` in exactly one place — `waits = WG.rows(st, cfg, time.time())` added at new lines 198–201, inside the function that builds the `data` mapping (`data["contested"] = contested`, `data["waiting"] = waits`, `data["taken_over"] = [{"id": ..., "holder": ..., "taken_over_by": ...}]`). But the new line `"waiting": [WG.line(w) for w in waits]` sits in a *different* return dict: its surrounding context builds its own `taken`/`contested` and renders `"taken_over": {i: by for i, (_holder, by) in taken.items()}` — a mapping, whereas the first function builds `data["taken_over"]` as a list of `{"id", "holder", "taken_over_by"}` records, and it also inserts `"contested"`/`"waiting"` conditionally (`if contested:`, `if waits:`) while the literal inserts them unconditionally. Those are two different payload shapes, i.e. two different functions.

`waits` is assigned inside the first function, so it is a local of that function; the second function has no `waits` binding (and the module defines none). A list comprehension is evaluated eagerly when the dict literal is constructed, so calling the function that returns this literal evaluates `[... for w in waits]` on every invocation, waiter or not, and raises `NameError: name 'waits' is not defined` at line ~243. Concretely: any caller of that overview/report function (e.g. rendering the payload for `ddflow overview`) crashes before returning, because `waits` was defined only in the sibling function.

chunk_findings.detail: The new verbatim whitelist registers `holder`, `lease_event` and `on` for `lease.waiting`, but not the fields that carry the waiter's own request: `globs` (and the agent ids inside `queue`). The same change's own comment in `ddflow/core/records.py` declares the record as `{"holder", "globs", "on", "since", "queue", "ttl_s", "lease_event", "agent", "at"}`, and the author protected the sibling values for exactly this reason — `holder` is annotated "an agent id compared with a lease's holder" and `on` is annotated "…glob pairs of the leases waited for", i.e. agent ids and glob values are values the redactor rewrites when the event is written to the log. Concrete input: agent W is refused and asks for `globs=["src/**/*.py"]`; `services/waiting.register` writes a `lease.waiting` event, `holder`/`on` survive redaction but the path-like `globs` value is rewritten. The waiter's wanted globs exist nowhere else (its `lease_event` only names its *current* lease, which by definition does not contain the globs it was refused), so after replay from the log the read-time evaluation in `services.waiting` can no longer match W's request against the holder's lease globs or against other waiters' queued globs: the release step that "names the globs OTHER agents are waiting for" and the second-refusal cycle detection compare redacted-to-placeholder values, so the waiter is never told to release and the FIFO ordering in `queue` cannot be reconstructed. Severity is MEDIUM rather than HIGH because the wait still terminates via the `ttl_s`/lease check; what is lost is the intended progress-break and cycle-detection behaviour for any glob value the redactor touches.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py `LOG_VERBATIM_FIELDS`

chunk_findings.detail: The `lines += [...]` statement is indented inside the outer `for ln in lanes:` body (8 spaces, same level as the `if`), and its comprehension iterates `for ln in lanes` again — all lanes, for every lane. The result is that every wait line is emitted once per active lane instead of once. Concretely, with two active lanes A and B where A has a standing wait record, `build()`/render produces the outer loop twice and each pass re-scans both lanes, so A's wait line appears twice in the printed output; with N lanes it appears N times, and the listing's size grows as O(lanes × waits) rather than O(waits). The fix is to dedent the line out of the outer loop (or iterate only over the current `ln.waits`), since the comprehension already performs the full traversal itself.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/render.py:47

chunk_findings.detail:
`queue_ahead` only keeps a queued waiter's place while the wanted globs are still held (`edges`) *or* while `now - w["at"] <= cfg.lease.waiter_reservation_s`, where `at` is the timestamp of the last `lease.waiting` event that was **appended**. But the comment says the place is kept "for `waiter_reservation_s` after they free up (the time it needs to come back and take them)" — the code measures from the last append, not from the moment the globs freed, and for the primary use case in the intent (a widening wait) `at` is never refreshed at all: in `register`, the dedup condition ends in `(lease_event or now - prior["at"] < cfg.lease.ttl_s / 2)`, and `lease_event` is a non-empty string for a widening, so the whole clause is True and `register` returns `prior` **without appending**, leaving `at` at the time of the first refusal. (Widening waits have no heartbeat at all, since their life is bounded by the lease, so `at` can be hours old.)

Concrete failure: agent A holds `help.py` on item Y; agent B holds item X and queued a widening for `help.py` at t=0 (`--queue`, recorded with `at=0`); at t=600 A releases `help.py`; at t=601 agent C claims `help.py`. B's record still stands (`standing` keeps a widening wait while its lease is live and does not cover `help.py`), but `blockers` now returns no edges, and `601 - 0 > waiter_reservation_s`, so the `if edges or ...` test is False and B is skipped. C's own `item_id` has no `lease.waiting` record, so `cutoff = float("inf")` and the FIFO `w["since"] >= cutoff` test does not filter B either — C is granted the glob ahead of B and B is starved, exactly the outcome the per-glob FIFO was added to prevent. The same skew applies to claim waits, because `register` only re-appends (and therefore only refreshes `at`) once per `lease.ttl_s / 2`, so `now - at` is normally far larger than `waiter_reservation_s` even for a waiter that is actively re-requesting.

chunk_findings.detail: The refusal under test is invoked as `run_cli(repo, "update", "T1", "--globs", "src/a.py,docs/x.md", agent=HOLDER)` — with no `--queue`. The change's own spec says the wait registration is opt-in: "`ddflow update --globs` and `ddflow claim` take an optional `--queue`: the refusal registers a waiting_on record ... and returns at once." So a plain refused update without `--queue` must record nothing, which is exactly what the replaced assertion (`len(EventLog(repo, "reader").read_all()) == n, "a refused update recorded events"`) enforced. The new assertion instead requires exactly one `lease.waiting` event for that no-`--queue` invocation. Given T2 holds `docs/x.md` and HOLDER runs `update T1 --globs src/a.py,docs/x.md` without `--queue`, the specified behavior is zero new events; the test asserts one, so it either fails against a correct implementation or locks in unconditional wait registration, defeating the optional flag (and re-introducing hold-and-wait for callers who did not opt in). The test should pass `--queue` (or otherwise enable queueing) before asserting the `lease.waiting` record.
